stories.topic: The swimmer who opens and closes the series
stories.summary: Amit's proposed web series, The Reformers, opens with an overhead shot of a tiny glistening blue speck surrounded by land. The camera zooms down until the speck becomes a large swimming pool with a man doing laps. The scene recurs in quiet moments across nine or ten seasons: someone comes to speak to him, he answers, they leave, and he keeps swimming. It is also the very last scene. The swimmer is KP Krishnan, for whom swimming is non-negotiable. He once asked to step out of a long cabinet meeting for an hour just to swim. Amit's eight-hour interview with him took four sessions instead of three because one session, at a conference in Kochi, ran into his 6 pm swimming time.
stories.insight: Amit sees the habit as conviction applied to small routines as well as big causes. It also works as a metaphor for the reformer's life: you keep going alone, and interruptions come and go.
stories.quote: And to me this is a great metaphor, that you're swimming alone. You know, someone interrupts you at one point and you send him away, you continue to swim. And right at the end, the last scene, you're still swimming alone.

stories.topic: A Rhodes Scholarship and a handshake
stories.summary: In his memoir Backstage, Montek Singh Ahluwalia describes winning a Rhodes Scholarship. There were no mobile phones, so he got word to his mother and told his father in person. His father simply shook his hand and said 'congratulations', and that was all. Ajay adds that Montek travelled to Britain by ship, going first by train to Bombay. Amit observes that a voyage gives you time to gather your thoughts.
stories.insight: Montek doesn't dwell on the scene, but Amit says Indian men will recognise why it is moving: a generation's restraint, where the most important feelings go unspoken.
stories.quote: when he tells his father in person, all his father does is shake his hand and say congratulations. And that's it, because we are just not so expressive and there is so much unspoken there that kind of reverberates.

stories.topic: Narayana Murthy's licence for an obsolete computer
stories.summary: In 1983 Narayana Murthy of Infosys wanted to import state-of-the-art Data General computers with three removable 200 MB drives. He spent months travelling to the ministry in Delhi for an import licence. The licence came through just as Data General released a newer machine with 300 MB drives that was 30% cheaper. Because the licence was tied to the specific model number, he had to buy the older, costlier machine or start another months-long licence chase.
stories.insight: The licence raj did more than slow businesses down. It locked them into worse, more expensive technology just as the world was moving ahead.
stories.quote: gets a license at just about the time Data General releases a next machine where the three removable drives are 300 MB and which is 30% cheaper. So you would imagine he'll get that, but he can't get that because the license is now for that particular model number.

stories.topic: The satellite dish that started a software revolution
stories.summary: As Ajay recalls it, with the caveat that he may be slightly off, the first important software development centre in India set up by a global company was Texas Instruments'. It needed a satellite dish, and the state had to permit it. In the mid-to-late 1980s, Montek was one of the key people who pushed through permission to install the dish.
stories.insight: Turning points can depend on an insider clearing one absurd permission. A single dish approval marks the start of India's software story.
stories.quote: Voluntary transactions by consenting adults were very complicated. And that is the beginning of the great Indian software revolution.

stories.topic: Eighty people locked in the finance ministry basement
stories.summary: After the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis hit (Montek had already drafted a secret reform roadmap, the 'M document', around 1990), the reform budget had to be prepared in total secrecy. Eighty people were taken to the basement of the Ministry of Finance and kept there for eight days, senior officers included. Dormitory beds were set up and food was brought in. Only the most senior people, such as the finance minister or finance secretary, could come and go.
stories.insight: The 1991 reforms read like a grand political moment. On the ground they were drafted by people who gave up their freedom for a week so the work could be done before the budget.
stories.quote: Eighty people are taken to the basement of the Ministry of Finance and they're locked there for eight days because it has to be done in secrecy, you know, before the budget comes out.

stories.topic: The suit that smelled of India
stories.summary: NK Singh once told Ajay this story. In an elevator at the IMF, one man turned around without looking and asked the person behind him, 'You're from India, aren't you?' The reason he knew: India had banned imports of the proper dry-cleaning fluids as luxuries. Indian dry cleaners used bad petrochemicals that left a distinctive stink on suits, so anyone in a suit with that smell had to be from India.
stories.insight: Protectionism leaves physical traces on ordinary life. Ajay later calls such humiliations the 'psychic dynamite' that pushed India's elite toward reform.
stories.quote: dry cleaning in India was done with some bad petrochemicals, which left a distinctive stink on a suit. So if a suit had a certain smell, then it meant that that person was from India.

stories.topic: The prime minister who coded in COBOL
stories.summary: PV Narasimha Rao, born around 1920, knew about ten languages, including Telugu, Hindi, Marathi, Kannada, Urdu and Persian. When computers arrived in India in the 1980s, he was a minister, and he taught himself computer languages: he could code fluently in COBOL and BASIC and wrote for Unix. Delhi still never took him seriously, partly because it doesn't take the South seriously and partly because its idea of refinement was skin-deep. Vinay Sitapati's chapter titles in Half-Lion ('Andhra's Socialist', 'Puppet Chief Minister', 'Delhi Darbar') trace his many reinventions.
stories.insight: What Amit admires more than learning is the capacity to keep learning and reinventing yourself. Delhi's markers of sophistication missed exactly that.
stories.quote: learning and refinement for Delhi means a very superficial things of how you speak English and how you hold your cup, and have you read some particular uh uh book that might be in vogue.

stories.topic: How Narasimha Rao got the job by not wanting it
stories.summary: After Rajiv Gandhi's death, the Congress fought over who would lead. The post was first offered to Vice President Shankar Dayal Sharma, who declined because he would rather become President later, as he did. Narasimha Rao got the top job because he was seen as not trying for it, which made him acceptable to everyone. Vinay Sitapati argues that his greatest quality was his loneliness: his ideal evening was reading or learning something new, not politicking.
stories.insight: History turns on accidents, and on the odd advantage of being the person who isn't scheming. Rao could play the power game, but his detachment is what made him the consensus choice.
stories.quote: His greatest quality was his loneliness.

stories.topic: 'You just apply. Leave the rest to me.'
stories.summary: Narasimha Rao met Akio Morita, chairman of Sony. He leaned over and almost whispered that millions of Indians dreamed of nothing more than owning a Sony television, so why not set up a factory in India? Morita gently replied that he would need so many licences that he would never get them. Rao leaned in further and answered in an even softer voice.
stories.insight: Rao was not merely managing the politics while others did the reforms. He was a true believer who personally pushed investment past the licence raj.
stories.quote: You just apply. Leave the rest to me.

stories.topic: A half-burnt pyre for a reforming prime minister
stories.summary: When Narasimha Rao died in 2004 he was already an outcast in his own party, and the Congress did not let his body be brought to Delhi for a state funeral. As Vinay Sitapati describes in Half-Lion, television channels that night showed his half-burnt pyre in Hyderabad, with his skull partly exposed and stray dogs coming at the remains.
stories.insight: Amit argues the Congress should proudly claim the 1991 liberalisation. Instead, petty politics disowned the man whose actions lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty, which makes Amit angry.
stories.quote: This was one of the greatest Indians of the twentieth century, who you know, whose actions helped lift hundreds of millions of people out of poverty.

stories.topic: 'Saamagri taiyaar hai': a nuclear handover
stories.summary: In his tribute after Narasimha Rao's death, Atal Bihari Vajpayee revealed a private exchange from May 1996. As Rao handed over power, he told Vajpayee that the material was ready, meaning the nuclear test. Rao's government had prepared it, but with elections underway it left the decision to the next government.
stories.insight: This was grace across party lines: Rao did the groundwork and left the credit to a successor.
stories.quote: They wanted it to happen. But there were elections and they had the grace to leave it for the next government.

stories.topic: Chidambaram's note on file: leave it to my successor
stories.summary: Ajay explains that when the RBI was created in 1934, its Act called it a temporary measure; in his telling, the British had no idea what they were doing. The real framework only arrived in 2015 with the monetary policy framework agreement signed by Rajiv Mehrishi and Raghuram Rajan. The inflation-targeting work was hatched in 2013 and agreed at file level by Montek, Manmohan Singh and P Chidambaram. With elections coming, Chidambaram wrote on file that such a momentous change should not be rushed through by a lame-duck administration, and left it to his successor. Arun Jaitley then implemented it.
stories.insight: Complex, multi-year reforms survive when outgoing governments refuse to rush them and incoming ones refuse to bin them.
stories.quote: It should not be rushed through in the late months of a lame duck administration. So I leave this to my successor.

stories.topic: Arun Jaitley: 'Who am I to disagree?'
stories.summary: From Amit's interview with KP Krishnan: in the 2000s, Krishnan and 'a certain young man called Ajay Shah' were seen as heretics for constantly pushing inflation targeting. When the new government came in, Krishnan gave the document to Arun Jaitley, who said the next morning, 'Let's go with it.' Krishnan urged him to think about the ramifications of something so radical. Jaitley felt insulted, as if he were being called unthoughtful, and then explained why he was confident.
stories.insight: It is unusual and admirable for a minister to defer openly to the judgement of political rivals on a technical question.
stories.quote: listen, two of India's finest legal and economic minds have said yes to this. Who am I to this agree?

stories.topic: Isher Judge's Hindi-medium climb
stories.summary: Isher Judge came from a conservative Sikh family and went to an all-girls, Hindi-medium Marwari school in Calcutta, in a world where higher education abroad was unthinkable. She went to Presidency College and then moved to Delhi, where she initially struggled with English, the language all the economics was written in. She was suspicious of slick Delhi boys with accents, but Montek's sense of humour won her over. They courted by watching Godard, Truffaut and Bresson films, and she became a fine economist in her own right. Amit regrets keeping her memoir, Breaking Through, unread and never inviting her on his show before she died.
stories.insight: The reformers shared a restless curiosity about the world. For Isher, getting into the conversation at all meant first conquering a language barrier.
stories.quote: And she had trouble for a few months uh figuring out English well enough because this all girls Marwari school she went to was Hindi medium.

stories.topic: Padma Desai, erased by alphabetical order
stories.summary: Padma Desai co-wrote a seminal 1968 book with Jagdish Bhagwati that argued against India's state-controlled system. His name comes first only because of alphabetical order, yet search results credit the book to him alone. She studied the Soviet Union for years and wrote a respected 1989 book on perestroika. Trapped in an abusive first marriage and denied a divorce, she used one of the legal grounds available, change of religion, and converted to Christianity so she could marry Bhagwati. Her memoir is Breaking Out.
stories.insight: The women among the reformers fought the same intellectual battles as the men while also fighting for recognition and for basic control over their own lives.
stories.quote: So she converted to Christian Christianity just to be able to marry uh the lover for life.

stories.topic: The panel that vanished during the Lehman collapse
stories.summary: Amit imagines the season on the 2008 crisis opening in a dimly lit Delhi basement with no phone signal. Ajay is moderating a panel with KP Krishnan of the finance ministry, RBI governor Subbarao and SEBI chief Bhave. One by one, someone walks up and whispers to each of them, and they get up and leave. Finance Minister Chidambaram, unable to reach any of their phones after Lehman Brothers collapsed, had got through to their drivers instead.
stories.insight: When a crisis breaks, the people actually running the system disappear from public view. Amit says the story of how they handled 2008 deserves one or two seasons of its own.
stories.quote: And you're suddenly moderating a conversation with no participants. You're all alone there, wondering what the hell happened.

stories.topic: Watching one stock price through the night
stories.summary: Ajay had planned a conference months in advance for 14–15 September 2008. On the 13th, as Lehman was filing for bankruptcy, Indian markets were turbulent and a small run seemed to be forming on ICICI Bank. ICICI's stock was only slightly down when the NSE closed at 3:30 pm. Ajay stayed up for hours watching the price of ICICI's ADR in New York, since all the evening's news would show up there. It barely moved, so he went to sleep. By the time his conference began in a basement at the IHC, Lehman had collapsed and Bombay's money market was choking.
stories.insight: In a crisis, situational awareness is hard, because the loudest voices often have an axe to grind. A market price can be a cleaner signal than the rumours.
stories.quote: There is a fog of war. At the time you actually don't know a whole lot of what's going on, and many of the people speaking the most uh loudly about the subject have an ax to grind.

stories.topic: Sushma Swaraj's plan to oppose in public
stories.summary: KP Krishnan told Amit about the New Pension Scheme, which was prepared under the Vajpayee government and handed to the Manmohan Singh government, which embraced it. Sitting across the table from Sushma Swaraj, then in opposition, the government side explained the scheme. She said it was wonderful and good for the country, warned that she would have to oppose it publicly in Parliament, and then laid out a step-by-step strategy for getting it passed anyway.
stories.insight: Adversarial politics in public can sit alongside private cooperation on what's good for the country, a quiet kind of statesmanship that fills Amit's heart with joy.
stories.quote: But let me tell you something, in public, because I'm in the opposition, if you bring it to parliament, I will have to oppose it.

stories.topic: How a terror attack reshuffled economic policy
stories.summary: Drawing on Puja Mehra's The Lost Decade, Amit traces a chain of accidents. After the 2008 Bombay attacks, Home Minister Shivraj Patil proved inadequate, so Manmohan Singh moved his best man, Chidambaram, to the home ministry. Sonia Gandhi got Pranab Mukherjee installed at finance, and when Manmohan went in for an operation, Pranab stayed on. He was a disaster as finance minister, bringing in retrospective taxation among other things, and was later 'kicked upstairs' to the presidency.
stories.insight: Economic trajectories can turn on personnel shuffles caused by unrelated events. A security crisis ended up derailing the reform momentum.
stories.quote: And he was a complete disaster as a finance minister, did things like retrospective taxation and various other things

stories.topic: The postcard that won over Pranab Mukherjee
stories.summary: KP Krishnan needed a financial-sector reform that Pranab Mukherjee's 1970s socialist instincts would reject. He prepared a two-slide presentation. The first slide was a postcard to Pranab from a constituent in Bengal, Sharmishtha Bandopadhyay, describing how her life savings had been wiped out and asking him to do something. Pranab had it read aloud and grew furious, demanding to know what Krishnan wanted. Krishnan explained that the current system was ruining ordinary people like her and proposed the reform. Seen that way, Pranab approved it on the spot.
stories.insight: Financial reform bores most audiences, so reformers have to show its effect on one real, named person to get it through.
stories.quote: Why are you reading this out for me? What do you want?

stories.topic: Recruitment by Jedi hand wave
stories.summary: Vijay Kelkar, then working in Geneva, ran into Manmohan Singh in a corridor at a Kathmandu conference around 1974. Manmohan simply said Kelkar would come and work with them; Kelkar felt obliged to say yes, an offer letter followed, and he moved to India. Kirit Parikh took two years to relocate: he worked first at the Atomic Energy Commission, and after Vikram Sarabhai died, he asked his recruiter whether the offer still stood and was told to come whenever he liked. Ajay introduced Viral Shah to Nandan Nilekani at an NCAER conference, and by that evening Nandan had offered Viral a job at UIDAI. Rakesh Mohan once phoned Ajay on a Thursday evening asking him to fly to Delhi the next morning to discuss joining the finance ministry, and Ajay said yes.
stories.insight: Much of India's reform talent arrived through personal pulls from people with conviction rather than formal hiring. There's a small recruitment story behind each of these careers.
stories.quote: So you will come to work with us, won't you?

stories.topic: Krishnan's first day was Ajay's last
stories.summary: In 2005, KP Krishnan, who had been a legend in the world of water supply and whom Ajay knew from a water conference, burst into Ajay's office at the Ministry of Finance to announce he had just joined as a joint secretary. Ajay had to tell him it was his last day; he was packing his boxes. It was also the day Ajay's mother died.
stories.insight: A bittersweet near-miss: two people who would later be linked on reforms like inflation targeting crossed paths on the day one of them was leaving.
stories.quote: And it was also the day my mother died. I was packing my boxes and uh leaving the ministry of finance.

stories.topic: Opening up petroleum, one piece at a time
stories.summary: When Vijay Kelkar became an adviser to the petroleum ministry, the state had a complete monopoly over exploration, extraction, refining, distribution and petrochemicals. Kelkar, the economist, worked closely with Secretary Lavraj Kumar, who knew how to work the bureaucratic and political machine. Both believed state monopolies made no sense. When Lavraj Kumar's tenure ended, Kelkar, though not from the IAS, became petroleum secretary and held the post for six years across governments. Over that time exploration, extraction, refining and petrochemicals were opened to the private sector; distribution fumbled.
stories.insight: Reform takes years of teamwork between strategic economists and skilled bureaucrats, plus a system that lets them stay on across governments. Ajay says this capability is no longer working the way it used to.
stories.quote: But that long journey of doing many, many things takes many years.

stories.topic: Manmohan's whisper to Naushad Forbes
stories.summary: Around 1991–92, Manmohan Singh explained his reform ideas at a meeting with industry leaders. Naushad Forbes sat between Ambani and JRD Tata (or so Amit recalls), producing a famous photograph that left everyone asking who the man in the middle was. Forbes had spoken in support of reform during the meeting. As they shook hands afterwards, Manmohan held on, pulled him a little closer, and whispered a request.
stories.insight: Even the finance minister driving the reforms had to recruit public advocates one at a time, because almost nobody outside understood or backed them.
stories.quote: tell the world everything you said today inside here.

recommendations.item: Backstage
recommendations.creator: Montek Singh Ahluwalia
recommendations.context: Montek's memoir, the source of the Rhodes-scholarship handshake and the tea scene with cabinet secretary BG Deshmukh.
recommendations.reason: A good memoir of the reform years, full of human detail about what working inside the system was like.

recommendations.item: Half-Lion
recommendations.creator: Vinay Sitapati
recommendations.context: Amit's main source for the Narasimha Rao chapter: his languages, coding, rise to power and funeral.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it fabulous. It shows Rao as a great man of learning and constant reinvention, not just a politician who happened to be there in 1991.

recommendations.item: Breaking Through
recommendations.creator: Isher Judge Ahluwalia
recommendations.context: Isher Judge Ahluwalia's autobiography, discussed in the chapter on women reformers.
recommendations.reason: A beautiful book about a Hindi-medium girl who became a fine economist. Amit regrets not reading it, and not recording with her, before she died.

recommendations.item: Breaking Out
recommendations.creator: Padma Desai
recommendations.context: Padma Desai's autobiography, discussed alongside Isher's.
recommendations.reason: The story of a remarkable economist and a strong woman who often goes uncredited. Amit says everyone should read it.

recommendations.item: The Lost Decade
recommendations.creator: Puja Mehra
recommendations.context: Cited for how reform stalled after the 2008 Bombay attacks.
recommendations.reason: Details the reshuffle that put Pranab Mukherjee in the finance ministry and decisions like retrospective taxation.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Mentioned while introducing Vijay Kelkar as Ajay's mentor and co-author.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it brilliant, a book on how economic policy should be made, by two people who were inside the reform story.

recommendations.item: The Struggle and the Promise
recommendations.creator: Naushad Forbes
recommendations.context: Amit isn't sure whether Manmohan Singh's 'tell the world' whisper appears in this book or came up in his podcast with Forbes.
recommendations.reason: Written by a business leader who backed reform publicly when few others did.

recommendations.item: The Logic of Collective Action
recommendations.creator: Mancur Olson
recommendations.context: Ajay invokes Olson's logic while explaining how India escaped 300% customs duties.
recommendations.reason: The classic account of concentrated interests beating dispersed beneficiaries. Ajay uses it to show what a purely political-economy view would predict, and why India defied that prediction.

recommendations.item: Lincoln
recommendations.creator: Steven Spielberg
recommendations.context: Ajay's response to the idea of a reform drama with nothing blowing up.
recommendations.reason: An eye-opener for Ajay. It skips Gettysburg and the war and stays on the legal battle to pass the 13th Amendment, and he finds it great storytelling.

recommendations.item: Kohrra
recommendations.creator: Sudip Sharma
recommendations.context: Amit's casting pitch for the series: Suvinder Vicky as Montek.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it a marvellous series and was so impressed by Suvinder Vicky's lead performance that he wants him to play Montek.

recommendations.item: Milestone
recommendations.creator: Ivan Ayr
recommendations.context: Danish Husain told Amit he first noticed Suvinder Vicky in this film.
recommendations.reason: The film where Suvinder Vicky first impressed Danish Husain, backing up Amit's casting choice.

recommendations.item: The Seen and the Unseen
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Ajay's closing recommendation, given in place of the usual book pick.
recommendations.reason: India hasn't yet done its economic history well, and Amit's long conversations with people like KP Krishnan and Montek are oral history, entry points into 'conversations with greatness'.

recommendations.item: The Soul of a New Machine
recommendations.context: Ajay recalls recommending it in an earlier episode on three firms, and links it to Narayana Murthy's Data General import saga.
recommendations.reason: It is about a design project inside Data General, the company whose computers Infosys spent months trying to import.

recommendations.item: The 1991 Project
recommendations.creator: Shruti Rajagopalan
recommendations.context: Mentioned while describing Montek's secret pre-crisis reform roadmap, the 'M document'.
recommendations.reason: A great website on 1991 that reproduces the legendary M document.

recommendations.reason: Amit calls it an epic piece of oral history, made possible by Ajay, and urges everyone to listen. It covers the reform process and the handling of the 2008 crisis in detail.

recommendations.reason: One of Amit's most popular episodes; he asks listeners to check it out alongside the book.

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Ajay Shah and Renuka Sane

recommendations.item: One Bad Law Goes, but Women Remain Second-Class Citizens

recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Cited while explaining why India's elite turned toward reform.

core_ideas.concept: The reforms as a second, silent freedom movement
core_ideas.explanation: India did not become fully free in 1947. For decades afterwards, economists and bureaucrats worked behind the scenes against their own incentives to dismantle an oppressive state, much as freedom fighters worked for principles with no immediate reward. The result lifted hundreds of millions out of poverty. Amit wants to tell it through human stories rather than policy, because every good story is a human story.
core_ideas.quote: bunch of people who were fighting behind the scenes in what I think is a great freedom movement.

core_ideas.concept: Sharpen the axe before the crisis
core_ideas.explanation: Amit cites the Abraham Lincoln line about spending five of six hours sharpening the axe before chopping a tree. People like Montek came back from lucrative jobs abroad to unglamorous advisory posts in the late 1970s and spent years preparing. When the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis opened a window, the ideas, the people and even a written roadmap (the M document) were ready.
core_ideas.quote: that old Abraham Lincoln quote, that if if if you give me six hours to chop a tree, I'll spend five hours sharpening the axe.

core_ideas.concept: Wounded pride as the engine of reform
core_ideas.explanation: After 1947, India's elite believed India was the post-colonial country most certain to succeed: the land of Tagore, Ramanujan, Nehru and Gandhi. The bad years from the 1962 China war to the Emergency, while Korea, Taiwan and Southeast Asia grew rich through openness, felt like a personal affront. That dissonance made former Marxists, including many Bengalis raised on land reform, rethink their views.
core_ideas.quote: So I think this was one powerful psychic force that was reshaping this community, saying, you know what, you may have been a Marxist when you were young, but it ain't working and you have to change course.

core_ideas.concept: Ideas, interests and institutions beat simple political economy
core_ideas.explanation: A pure Mancur Olson reading predicts that incumbents protected by 300% tariffs, with concentrated gains and the power to pay bribes, would never let tariffs fall. Yet India cut customs duties year after year until 2007–08. Ajay says this happened because the reformers read, argued and debated ideas, so policy didn't collapse into a contest between factions. Interests matter, but ideas and institutions can outplay them.
core_ideas.quote: But just year after year, the Indian political system was able to play this combination of ideas, interests, and institutions

core_ideas.explanation: Big reforms outlast single governments only when politicians act with restraint. Examples from this episode: Narasimha Rao left the nuclear test to Vajpayee; Chidambaram deferred inflation targeting to his successor; Jaitley adopted it; the pension scheme passed from Vajpayee's government to Manmohan's; Sushma Swaraj privately helped pass a reform she would publicly oppose.
core_ideas.quote: So that's the decency and grace by which we can build complex projects across elections.

core_ideas.concept: A stable professional elite as institutional memory
core_ideas.explanation: Ministers are temporary. Long reforms like opening up petroleum needed a professional elite of people such as Lavraj Kumar and Vijay Kelkar who could think, mentor and protect one another, and carry knowledge across changes of government. Ajay warns this capability is no longer working the way it used to.
core_ideas.quote: Ministers come, ministers go, but you need this stability of the professional elite public policy in India that is able to think and sustain each other and protect each other and become that institutional memory that carries knowledge across.

core_ideas.concept: Counterintuitive ideas need a long game
core_ideas.explanation: The reformers' core ideas, positive-sum games and spontaneous order, are hard to explain and easy to caricature: 'the state shouldn't do this' gets heard as 'he's anti-poor, pro-business'. With almost no public support, as shown when Manmohan Singh privately asked Naushad Forbes to speak up, these people still spent decades on the cause. Amit contrasts that with armchair columnists like himself.
core_ideas.quote: And yet, not for years, but for decades, these people don't do what people like me do, write columns and be armchair columnists, but for years and decades these people devote their lives to playing this long game.

core_ideas.concept: Put a human face on boring reforms
core_ideas.explanation: Financial reforms put audiences to sleep but shape everyone's life. KP Krishnan's postcard tactic with Pranab Mukherjee shows how to convert them: start with one named person whose savings the current system destroyed. Amit says reformers and storytellers both need to find ways to tell these stories.
core_ideas.quote: Now you can't talk about financial reforms to a large audience because it is so incredibly boring, right?

core_ideas.explanation: Amit sees a common trait in the reformers: refusing to accept the world as it is and wanting to understand it. Rao learned programming in middle age, and Isher and Montek courted by discovering European cinema together. What impresses Amit most is the ability to keep learning, more than learning itself.
core_ideas.quote: We are not happy with the way things are we want to know the world we want to figure it out.

core_ideas.explanation: The male reformers swam against the tide. Women like Isher Judge Ahluwalia and Padma Desai first had to break into ministries and academic departments run almost entirely by men. Amit sees a leftover of this today: almost every accomplished woman he invites on his podcast asks 'Why me?', while the men never do.
core_ideas.quote: The women are doubly remarkable because women are not in this game at all.

core_ideas.concept: Prices cut through the fog of war
core_ideas.explanation: During the Lehman weekend, rumours were everywhere and the loudest voices had agendas. Ajay relied on one signal, the ICICI ADR price in New York, because everything that had happened since the Indian market closed would be reflected in it. A traded price combines dispersed information better than any single person's opinion.
core_ideas.quote: So I vividly remembered that I was just waiting and waiting and waiting for the American market to open because I wanted to see the stock price of the ICICI ADR in America.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: After Ajay admits his taste in films is a 13-year-old's love of spectacle, Amit sums up the pair: 'You are the kind of person who likes to blow things up, and I'm the kind of person who wants to curl up in a corner and cry.'

The pilot's opening shot looks like a violent clash of colours until the camera pulls back to show someone spreading Marmite on toast. Ajay admits he hates Marmite, and Amit says 'So does the protagonist of this particular chapter.'

The opening scene is set in economist Balbir Singh's suite in Rudra North at St Stephen's in the early 1960s. Bade Ghulam Ali Khan plays tinnily on a recorder while the Oxford-returned professor talks music with students, and a shy young Montek sits at the back.
Ajay on the Texas Instruments satellite-dish saga: 'Voluntary transactions by consenting adults were very complicated.'
On the 80 officials locked in the finance ministry basement for eight days, Amit borrows the Hotel California line: 'you can check out but you can never leave.'

After Montek, a genteel and soft-spoken man, fielded question after question from the Joint Parliamentary Committee, a TV reporter asked an MP leaving the room how it went. His answer: 'Sardarji bahut bolte hain.' It also became a chapter title.
Ajay sets up the dry-cleaning story with 'if you are a male who is an unfortunate owner of a thing called a suit', noting that dry cleaning is how you signal class, since poor people can't afford it.
Ajay asks whether Narasimha Rao was a Gorbachev figure: deeply knowledgeable and also a master of the intrigue needed to win and hold power. Amit says he doesn't know enough about Gorbachev to judge.

On Shankar Dayal Sharma turning down the top job to become President later, Amit paraphrases: 'I can chill and be in the Rashtrapati Bhavan. Not in so many words, obviously, because I don't think Mr. Sharma would have said I can chill.'
Ajay on the RBI's origins: the 1934 Act called it a temporary measure because the British 'had no idea what they were doing', so 'the concept of the Reserve Bank of India really only began in 2015.'

Ajay recalls Jagdish Bhagwati telling a dinner table that his brother, PN Bhagwati, found out Jagdish and Padma Desai were 'living in sin' and grumbled that it was a crime under the IPC, 'so just be careful.'
Isher and Montek's courtship: watching European films by Godard, Truffaut and Bresson together.

Ajay calls Isher telling him his articulation was like young Montek's 'the sweetest thing that anybody ever said to me.' Amit: 'I'm sure young Montek's humour was better than yours.' Ajay: 'No doubt.'
Ajay announces 'Chapter three.' Amit: 'it's not actually chapter three. You're losing count. What kind of card carrying economist are you when you can't even count?'
As the panellists vanish one by one during the Lehman crisis, Amit says the audience doesn't mind 'because you're on stage and you're so beautiful and they're just looking at you lost in rapture.'
Ajay describes Manmohan Singh recruiting Vijay Kelkar in a Kathmandu corridor with 'a Jedi hand wave', the Star Wars mind trick, after which Kelkar simply felt obliged to say yes.
Amit calls In Service of the Republic 'the brilliant book' and wonders, 'Have we mentioned it before?' The answer: 'A couple of hundred times.'
Asked who should play him, Ajay recalls a student at ISB who once said he looked like someone from Hollywood, 'and I've forgotten the name.'
Ajay refers to the episode 'for which you have the enigmatic title, Why Freedom Matters, but it's actually an economic history piece', a dig at Amit's titling.
Ending his recommendation of Amit's podcast, Ajay signs off with 'we're at the end of this episode of The Seen and the Unseen.' Amit: 'We won't edit that out. It's a very nice fumble.'
